script_data.title: Why Your 'Common Sense' Isn't So Common
script_data.description: 🤯 Ever been absolutely POSITIVE your opinion was the popular one, only to be genuinely FLOORED when you found out most people disagreed? 😱 You thought it was common sense, an undeniable truth, right? 🤔 This brain glitch hits us all! 👇 Our minds are wired to assume agreement, creating a 'false consensus' that can lead to some truly shocking revelations. 🧠💡 Why do we do this? Is it ego? Is it just how our brains try to simplify a complex world? Join the discussion and share a time this happened to you! 👇
script_data.script:
Imagine you're scrolling through social media, and a hot topic dominates your feed: perhaps a new controversial policy, a viral celebrity scandal, or even the 'correct' way to load a dishwasher. You've formed a strong opinion, one that feels utterly rational, undeniably logical, and frankly, *obvious*. You share it with your friends, your family, or your online bubble, and everyone nods in agreement. “Of course,” you think, “anyone with half a brain cell would see it this way. This is just common sense.” You proceed with your day, utterly convinced that your perspective represents the broad consensus, the collective wisdom of the masses.

But then, you venture beyond your immediate echo chamber. You join an online forum with diverse viewpoints, read a news article from a different perspective, or simply overhear a group of strangers discussing the very same topic. Suddenly, you're hit with a wave of dissenting opinions. People vehemently disagree with your “common sense” view, offering counterarguments you hadn't even considered. Your initial reaction isn't just surprise; it's genuine bewilderment, perhaps even a touch of indignation. How can *so many* people be so wrong?

This profound shock is a classic demonstration of the **False Consensus Effect**, a pervasive cognitive bias where we overestimate the extent to which our beliefs, values, characteristics, and behaviors are typical of others. Your brain, in its efficiency, tends to project your internal world onto the external, assuming a shared reality that doesn't always exist. This isn't vanity; it's a mental shortcut. We often operate within social bubbles, both online and offline, where we primarily encounter individuals who reinforce our existing viewpoints. This fuels the **Availability Heuristic**, making similar opinions readily accessible and thus seeming more prevalent. Our minds also subtly engage **Confirmation Bias**, seeking out evidence that supports our existing beliefs and downplaying information that challenges them. From an evolutionary standpoint, assuming agreement within one's social group might have fostered cohesion and reduced conflict, making it a useful, albeit often misleading, heuristic for navigating complex social landscapes. Your brain doesn't maliciously mislead you; it simply takes the path of least resistance, preferring the comfortable illusion of agreement over the discomfort of confronting widespread divergence.

Is my opinion truly popular?
script_data.dilemma_seed: You're convinced your opinion on a popular topic is shared by most people, only to be genuinely shocked when you encounter widespread disagreement. Your brain projects your beliefs onto others.
